newsitem.title: USA: Republican governors put Clinton on notice.
newsitem.headline: Republican governors put Clinton on notice.

text.p: Republican governors, who control states with nearly three-quarters of the population, put President Clinton on notice Sunday that they will not let him back away from the "Republican ideas" that they said won him re-election.

"We have to watch very carefully what he does," said Gov. Christine Whitman of New Jersey, expressing fear Clinton would revert to "the old philosophy" of liberalism and big government, abandoning the more moderate agenda that won him a second term but left the House and Senate with Republican majorities.

The election was a "split decision," Michigan Gov. John Engler said, in which "Republican ideas" adopted by Clinton helped him beat Bob Dole. Clinton won because he convinced voters he "thought like a Republican," Iowa Gov. Terry Branstad said.

"Let me say a word to the President of the United States, who has talked a lot about building a bridge to the 21st Century," Gov. Stephen Merrill of New Hampshire said. "With all due respect, Mr. President, if you build that bridge it will land in Republican territory."

"The Republican agenda has already captured the hearts and minds of the future in this nation. So whenever that bridge is built and wherever it comes down it will be on Republican territory, as defined by smaller government and lower taxes and stronger values."

The bridge-building image was a central theme of Clinton's re-election campaign, one through which the 50-year-old president sought to portray himself as a link to the future and the 73-year-old Dole as a link to the past.

The governors spoke at a news conference opening the three-day annual meeting of the Republican Governors Association, where they will push for policy changes and reassess the election and their party's status, in company with Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and assorted members of Congress.

There are Republican governors in a record 32 states. Among them are some likely candidates for the party's presidential nomination in four years. About 25 of the Republican governors came to Michigan for the meeting.

Engler, current chairman of the association, said a top priority for the governors is passage of a constitutional amendment requiring a balanced budget -- a proposal that failed in the Senate during the last Congress. He predicted the party's increased strength in the Senate will reverse that outcome when the issue returns for another vote.

Engler said other issues of top concern to the governors are "streamlining the maze of federal job training programmes," which he said might be accomplished in the early days of the next Congress, limiting the "federal judiciary's power especially as it is exercised vis a vis the states," as well as Medicaid reform and the simplification and reduction of taxes.

Merrill said the governors are standing by to help Congress. "We've balanced budgets in all of our states, we've pushed welfare reform in all of our states and we're going to continue to do so," he said.
